newsitem.title: FRANCE: French industrial production hints at weak fourth quarter.
newsitem.headline: French industrial production hints at weak fourth quarter.

text.p: French industrial production fell sharply in October for the second month in a row, further evidence that the economy is set to end the year on a weak note, official figures released Friday showed.

Economists said the broad-based decline in output was bad news, and added that coupled with falls in consumer spending and enduring weak consumer sentiment, it could even translate into economic contraction in the fourth quarter of 1996.
Industrial production excluding energy dropped 0.8 percent in October from September, yielding a 1 percent year-on-year rise, national statistics institute INSEE reported.
Manufacturing output, which excludes energy, agri-food businesses and construction, fell 1.2 percent month-on-month but was 0.8 percent higher than a year ago.
"It's a very weak number. It supports our view that GDP (gross domestic product) will fall in the fourth quarter," said J.P. Morgan economist David Naude.
"What makes the number look ugly is that it comes after a big fall in September but also that it's very broad based and not just payback on the car front," Naude added.
In September, industrial production excluding construction fell 1.4 percent and manufacturing output was down 1.9 percent.

While the car industry suffered the biggest setback in October, with production dropping 3.1 percent as the positive effect of government-subsidised rebate programmes wore off, other sectors were also hard hit.
Consumer goods production and construction were also sharply lower, falling 2.6 and 2.1 percent respectively.
The report showed seven of the production index's nine elements fell in October. Only agri-food and energy eked out small gains of 0.9 percent and 0.2 percent respectively.

Economists said the weakness in consumer goods production was the most worrying part of the report because it reflected weak consumer spending and hinted production might well remain soft for the rest of the year.

"The consumer goods part is bad news because it confirms that it's more than just cars," said Smith Barney international economist Paul Horne. He added that levels of consumer spending remained disappointing.
"The consumer remains a problem," Horne said. "There's a lot of window shopping going on but that's pretty much it. November and December will remain weak."
INSEE reported preliminary figures on Nov. 28 that showed third-quarter GDP rose 0.9 percent after falling 0.2 percent in the second quarter.

Most economists have until recently been predicting a modest rise in fourth quarter GDP, but several said Friday that if there were no sign of improvement soon, they could revise down their forecasts to show a contraction.
"My reaction was to slightly cut my manufacturing output forecast for the fourth quarter," said Eric Chaney, economist with Morgan Stanley.
"I am sticking with plus 0.2 percent but it is on watch and I don't exclude having to revise it down," he said of his forecast for fourth quarter GDP.

Naude said that perhaps the most ominous sign was that the third quarter had ended badly. "If you look at where the quarter ended compared to where it started, it shows the economy was downwardly oriented by September," he said.
